messages.subject: Classify an unknown tissue
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
My name is Paco and I'm analysing my MSI data with Cardinal. Thank you for that great job.
At the moment I'm doing a supervised analysis of my data (like in the rcc example) for classification. As you say in the tutorial the goal of the workflow is to develop classifiers for predicting whether a new tissue sample is normal or cancer. I have a set of tissues identified as cancerous or normal by our pathologists. I used this set of MSI data for training the classifier using the three methods described. So at this point a suppose that hopefully I have a unique chemical profiles for normal tissue and cancerous tissue. So the question is... What's next? How can I predict the class of a new sample? What's the way to load an unidentified tissue and use the classifier to predict the class to which it belongs?
Thanks in advance
Paco

messages.subject: Re: Classify an unknown tissue
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paco,

Thanks for using Cardinal! To predict on a new dataset, you use the predict() method with the trained classifier. So assuming, you've trained a classifier and you call it, say, myClassifier, it would go like, for example:

myDataset <- readMSIData("myFile.extension")
# ... do some pre-processing ... #
myClassifier <- spatialShrunkenCentroids(myDataset, y=myResponse) # or PLS or OPLS
myNewDataset <- readMSIData("myNewFile.extension")
# ... do some pre-processing ... #
myPrediction <- predict(myClassifier, newx=myNewDataset)

Keeping in mind, of course, that the training data and the new data will need to have the same m/z values.

-Kyle

messages.subject: Reducing x,y imaging coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

I was wondering if you have already built into Cardinal a method for reducing x,y dimension to the smallest possible displayable size? (x = x- (min(x)-1),y = y- (min(y)-1)) I don't see it in the reference manual?

This is really useful for Bruker imaging data where the x and y values maybe something like 200-400 and 700-800, so rescaling them to between 0-200 removes empty space in the plot space and significantly speeds up plotting time, especially when you have several imaging acquisitions in the msset.

I have written my own function for this below, but I'm sure you could implement something much more direct as mine is kind of a workaround and requires parsing the data into a data.frame, splitting it, etc. Probably way more steps than are necessary.

reduceCardinalCoord<- function(cardinaldata){
  df<- data.frame(t(iData(cardinaldata)))
  colnames(df) <- cardinaldata@featureData@data$mz
  df$x <- cardinaldata@pixelData@data$x
  df$y <- cardinaldata@pixelData@data$y
  df$sample <- cardinaldata@pixelData@data$sample
  dfs <- split(df, df$sample)
  for(i in 1:length(dfs)){
    dfs[[i]]$x <- dfs[[i]]$x - (min(dfs[[i]]$x) - 1)
    dfs[[i]]$y <- dfs[[i]]$y - (min(dfs[[i]]$y) - 1)
  }
  df <-do.call(rbind, dfs)
  msset <- MSImageSet(spectra=t(df[,1:length(cardinaldata@featureData@data$mz)]), coord=df[c("x","y","sample")], mz=as.numeric(colnames(df[1:length(cardinaldata@featureData@data$mz)])))
  processingData(msset) <- processingData(cardinaldata)
  return(msset)
}

Anyway, thanks again for the package, it's very useful,

Heath

messages.subject: Re: Reducing x,y imaging coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Heath,

Thank you again for using Cardinal!

For a 1-sample dataset, the image() method should automatically crop the image to the appropriate coordinate limits. As you've found out, for multiple-sample datasets, the image() method crops the dataset to the max coordinate limits for the entire dataset, which may not be the best limits for each individual sample.

I've been thinking of a better way to handle this, and including an option for automatically cropping images on a per-sample basis in the image() method. This will probably happen when I have time to implement better handling of 3D datasets, since it makes sense to crop images on a per-sample basis for 2D datasets, but to plot 3D datasets with the same x-y limits for all samples (the current default).

I think it makes the most sense to make this an option in the image() method for how default image plotting is handled, rather than providing a function for automatically cropping coordinates in a dataset, which I think is better left to the user.

In the meantime, you needn't create a whole new dataset to accomplish what you're trying to do. Using the coord() method will save you several lines of code.

For the rcc dataset in CardinalWorkflows, for example, you can do:

library(CardinalWorkflows)

data(rcc)

for ( samp in sampleNames(rcc) ) {
s <- pData(rcc)$sample %in% samp
coord(rcc)$x[s] <- coord(rcc)$x[s] - min(coord(rcc)$x[s]) + 1
coord(rcc)$y[s] <- coord(rcc)$y[s] - min(coord(rcc)$y[s]) + 1
}

(You can speed this up slightly by saving the whole coord() data.frame, editing it on its own, and replacing it all at once using coord()<-.)

-Kyle
